analysis.one_liner: Taxes half of oil and gas companies' excess profits to fund low-income energy aid and veterans' health care.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2005, referred to four House committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have placed a 50% excise tax on "windfall profits" from oil and natural gas — profits above a company's average profit from 2000-2004 plus 10%. It would also tax net gains from trades whose prices are tied to oil and gas. Half the money raised would go to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills, and half to Department of Veterans Affairs medical services. It applied to tax years 2005 and 2006.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households who receive help paying energy bills through LIHEAP, and veterans who rely on VA medical services, would gain new dedicated funding. The money would come from oil and gas companies' profits above their recent historical levels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income energy aid recipients and veterans

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on windfall profits from sales of crude oil, natural gas, and their products, defined as profits above the taxpayer's average 2000-2004 profit plus 10% [S2].
Also taxes net gains from financial transactions whose prices are determined by reference to crude oil or natural gas prices, capturing speculation on energy price spikes [S2].
Appropriates 50% of the revenue to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and 50% to Department of Veterans Affairs medical services [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and natural gas producers and energy traders, whose profits above their 2000-2004 average would be taxed at 50%. Some of the cost could be passed to consumers through higher prices, though the tax's deductibility and the profit baseline soften the effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and traders

drawbacks.text: A windfall tax on producers can be passed along to consumers in the form of higher prices, partially offsetting the aid it funds; the bill allowed the tax to be deducted for income tax purposes, which also reduces its net revenue [S3].
The profit baseline — average 2000-2004 profits plus 10% — is an arbitrary benchmark that could penalize companies whose growth was legitimate rather than driven by price spikes [S2].
Taxes that target a single industry's excess profits can discourage investment in future energy production, a standard objection to windfall profit taxes generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directed money to two clear public needs — low-income energy assistance and veterans' medical care — and paid for it by taxing profits above an industry's recent historical norm. The main honest objections are that some cost could reach consumers through prices and that the baseline could catch legitimate growth. But as a response to the 2005 energy price spike, the benefits to low-income households and veterans outweighed the design flaws; the larger flaw is that it never received any consideration.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees, then to subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on November 9, 2005, with Rep. Rosa DeLauro as its sole cosponsor [S1].
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Veterans' Affairs committees on the day of introduction [S5].

In the following weeks and months it was referred to the Health, Energy and Air Quality, and Education Reform subcommittees; no committee or subcommittee ever reported it, and the full House never voted on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and natural gas companies were better off, since their windfall profits from the 2005 price spike went untaxed, and low-income households and veterans received no new dedicated funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers kept their windfall profits

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued it with a mechanism routing oil windfall tax revenue to LIHEAP and veterans' medical care.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of primary referral; controls whether tax bills get a markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it was sent to a subcommittee and never reported out.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the House floor agenda in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor at any point in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and with Republican majorities in the House it never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would have taxed 50% of their profits above a 2000-2004 baseline, directly clawing back the windfall from the 2005 price spike. The industry's interest in avoiding the tax ran against the households the revenue would have funded.
Net gains from financial transactions tied to crude oil and natural gas prices would also have been taxed at 50%, targeting profits made from betting on energy price increases.

industries.industry: Low-income energy assistance and veterans' health programs
industries.note: LIHEAP and VA medical services would have received equal dedicated shares of the tax revenue, giving both a funding stream tied to energy industry profits.
